rising electricity bills has become a flashpoint

The Consumer Price Index for electricity has surged by 6.7% year-over-year and by 41% overall since January 2020, higher than the rate of inflation over this period.23 This increase comes at a time of growing national anxiety about “affordability,” a concern that already includes energy prices along with the rising costs of other basic goods and services.24

25 About 4% of all U.S. electricity in 2025 was consumed by data centers,26 and multiple independent forecasts show this share rising sharply—potentially doubling or tripling over the next decade depending on AI-driven load growth.
By 2026-2027, data centers are expected to consume 6-8% of all U.S. electricity, with the data center share increasing to 8-12% by 2030 and 10-18%
2050.27 According to one projection, data centers will account for
of all U.S. load growth through 2030,28 meaning that half of all increases in U.S. power production will be data center-driven
29 Consumers are concerned about not only the magnitude of these costs, but whether they will be distributed equitably among ratepayers.
Activist groups and local officials have repeatedly warned that utility rate-bases may subsidize grid
and capacity additions that serve data centers but not the public at large,

Another growing grassroots concern is the huge quantity of water required by data centers to cool servers and other equipment. According to studies, a 150-MW hyperscale data center using evaporative cooling consumes roughly 340,000 gallons per day—or about 124 million gallons per year.31 It is estimated that U.S. data centers used 17.4 billion gallons of water in 2023 and that consumption will reach 38-73 billion gallons by 2028. Indirectly, data center growth will also increase cooling water requirements at power plants as new fossil fuel generating capacity is built to power data centers.32 Technologies like closed-loop water recycling can reduce water consumption and safeguard local water resources but may require increased energy utilization, imposing higher energy costs and increasing power plant air emissions.33

By siphoning off water from public systems, data centers may add to water scarcity in regions with constrained supplies.34 In this event, not only would water bills be higher but, in the worst case, it may be necessary to impose rationing or other curbs on water use, placing severe hardships on businesses and residents.
V. The Congressional and White House Response

The community voices raising the alarm about data centers are finding an audience in Washington, D.C. President Trump has been a vocal supporter of data centers and unfettered AI, but has tried to defuse grassroots concern about escalating energy costs through his voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge.35 This Pledge would commit data center developers and technology companies to cover the incremental increases in electricity costs tied to new power capacity serving data center electricity demand. Some 200 companies and nearly all Republican state governors have now signed the Pledge36; however, critics have cautioned that it is unenforceable and lacks mechanisms to track whether data center owners are meeting their commitments.37

To fill this void, both houses of Congress are now working on the Ratepayer Protection Act, bipartisan legislation requiring states to consider adopting a federal standard that would compel data centers to pay the total cost of new generation and transmission upgrades to connect them to the grid, protecting consumers from bearing these costs through their electricity bills.38 The U.S. House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee recently approved the bill unanimously, and it may reach the House floor later this year.39
VI. The Need to Do More

While supporting this legislation, some leading Democrats, along with advocates, community groups, and state legislators, are warning that it fails to address the full range of data center concerns and calling for more ambitious action.40 A proposal gaining traction is a nationwide moratorium on data center construction,41 similar to the one adopted by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul42 and now by Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.43 Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), the influential ranking minority member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, recently backed this concept. Warning that “We’re seeing electricity prices sky rocketing, the grid is strained, and there is also a lot of concern about clean air and water pollution, and most states don’t have anything on the books,” Pallone said “there needs to be guardrails” to address these concerns but, “if we can’t achieve that, then the possibility of a moratorium out there is certainly real.”44

A pause in data center construction is anathema to those who, like the president, believe the United States is in an existential race with China for global AI hegemony and will lose that race if we pull back from rapid buildout of data centers.45 But even without a moratorium, we can’t assume the path ahead for new data centers will be smooth and seamless. What if the proliferation of data centers will strain our energy and water systems to the breaking point? Or if air quality and public health will be compromised by hundreds of new highly polluting power plants? Or if many of the new centers on the drawing board will never be built because state and local governments, egged on by angry citizens, block them? Wouldn’t this constitute a de facto moratorium, even if there’s no official embargo on data center construction?
The fears of data center opponents are not merely hypothetical concerns of hand-wringing alarmists.
The threat of data centers to our electrical supply systems is real and imminent.
We know the rapid increase in data center construction projected over the next 15 years will demand dramatic increases in energy supply.

, electric utilities that are already struggling to manage supply-and-demand imbalances will be unable to serve their customers. Grid operators with constrained reserve margins will then be hard-pressed to maintain system reliability, and
, brownouts, and other disruptions in service
may be more frequent and widespread.

Even if sufficient new generation capacity is constructed and connected to the grid, the costs will be huge and, if passed on to ratepayers, will accelerate electricity price increases and raise the rate of inflation.

similar to the oil shocks of the 1970s
Because of political gridlock and long-standing structural flaws in our energy supply system, the United States is grossly unprepared to meet a new surge in electricity demand.

The PJM interconnection,46 the grid operator for the heavily populated Mid-Atlantic region and parts of the Midwest, is home to more data centers than any other region.47 But PJM’s power reserves are already too small to meet reliability requirements,48 and during a recent summer heat wave, power demand reached 163 gigawatts (GW),49 the secondhighest level on record, and would have been higher if PJM had not ordered curtailments of energy use.

PJM has acknowledged that significant new capacity is needed just to meet the energy needs of data centers now operating,50 and it projects that data centers alone will add over 30 GW of additional peak electricity demand by 2030.51 In Virginia, the national epicenter of data center construction and part of PJM, Dominion Energy, the dominant utility, has estimated that new data centers in the pipeline will need 70,000 MW of power if they come online.52

Worried power suppliers and federal and state energy regulators are well aware of PJM’s vulnerabilities and working overtime to remedy them.53 But the challenges are immense and there are few fixes that are readily implementable.

and proposals to build new centers are on hold because of grid constraints

PJM’s woes are not unique. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, another hotbed of data center development, just announced that demand on the state’s main power grid could nearly double in the next five to six years, almost entirely due to new data centers, and that only a fraction of that demand could be met using available or projected power generation.55 In response, Republican Governor Abbott halted new applications to connect data centers to the grid.56

At the national level, policymakers understand that growth in electricity demand cannot be met unless we reform our energy supply system to address its deeply rooted shortcomings.57 These include lack of incentives and drivers for building new transmission lines across state lines; delays in building interconnections that give new load centers access to the grid; logjams in permitting and environmental approvals; and inadequate federal and state funding for investments in grid modernization. These issues are unresolved not because Congress isn’t trying, but because they are complex and politically divisive and longterm solutions are difficult to design and implement.
